parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin -archa, from Latin -archēs, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”, “government”).
Inherited from Late Latin -attus (second declension).
Inherited from Late Latin -ittus. Doublet of -ete.
Inherited from Old Spanish -izar, a learned borrowing from Late Latin -izāre. Doublet of -ear, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Late Latin -mantia, from Ancient Greek μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

parole.significato: -ment; forms nouns from verbs with the sense of the action or process
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish -miento. Doublet of -mento.

parole.significato: forms adjectives that signify relation to the word stem
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -iscus.
Borrowed from Late Latin abacista, from Latin abacus (“abacus”) + -ista (“-ist”).

parole.significato: abbess (female superior of a nunnery or convent)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish abbadesa, from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbatissa, from Latin abbas (“abbot”).
Borrowed from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbātia, based on Latin abbas (“abbot”).

parole.significato: to bring down, to shoot down
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish abatir (“to bring down”), from Late Latin abbattere, from Latin battere. Compare English abate.
Borrowed from Late Latin abdicatīvus.

parole.significato: alphabet (an ordered set of letters used in a language)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin abecedārium, from abecedārius (“alphabetical”).
Borrowed from Late Latin abōminābilis.

parole.significato: to bundle up, to keep someone warm
parole.testo: From Late Latin apricāre, from Latin aprīcārī (“warm in the sun”), from aprīcus (“sunny”) Compare Portuguese abrigar, Catalan abrigar, English apricate, French abrier. Alternatively, from Late Latin *abrigāre (“to cover, shelter”), from a- + brigare, from Frankish *biwrīhan (“to cover, protect”), fr
Borrowed from Late Latin abstentiōnem, from Latin abstentus, from abstineō.
Borrowed from Late Latin abstractiōnem, equivalent to abstracto + -ción.
Inherited from Late Latin aviola, diminutive from Latin avia.
Borrowed from Late Latin accessibilis (“accessible”), from accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach”).
Borrowed from Late Latin accidēntālis.

parole.significato: sorrel (Rumex acetosa, common sorrel plant with acidic leaves, used for seasoning salad due to its sour taste)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin acētāria (“vegetables prepared with oil and vinegar; vinaigrette seasoned greens; salad”).

Inherited from Old Spanish azero (“steely”, adjective), from Late Latin aciārium. Cognate with Asturian aceru, Catalan acer, French acier, Galician aceiro, Italian acciaio, Occitan acièr, and Portuguese aço.
From Late Latin acētōsus, from Latin acētum.

Borrowed from Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos).
Inherited from Late Latin addormīre.
Borrowed from Late Latin adversatīvus.
From the noun adonio, from Late Latin adonius, from Latin adonium (“Adonic verse”).

parole.significato: aphorism (short phrase conveying some principle or concept of thought)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós).
Inherited from Late Latin aquamanīle, from Latin aqua (“water”), and the root of manus (“hand”). Compare Portuguese gomil, agomil.
Inherited from Old Spanish aguja, from Late Latin acūcula, diminutive of Latin acus (“needle”). Compare Sicilian agugghia.
Borrowed from Late Latin adfiliare, affiliare (“to adopt as a son”), from Latin ad + filius (“son”). Compare Portuguese afilhar, Asturian afiar, Italian affiliare. Doublet of afiliar.
Inherited from Late Latin alapārī (“to boast”), originally (in Plautus) “to slap”, which is probably related to Latin alapa (“box on the ear, blow with the hand”).

parole.significato: wire (metal formed into a long, narrow thread)
parole.testo: From Old Spanish alambre, arambre, aramne (“bronze”), from Late Latin aerāmen, derived from Latin aes.
Borrowed from Late Latin Albigēnsis, Albigenses.
Borrowed from Late Latin alborem, from Latin albus.
From albo + -ura, or taken from Late Latin albūra, from Latin albus. Compare Portuguese alvura.
From Late Latin allēgorizāre.

parole.significato: large haystack kept in storage, often with a pole through its centre
parole.testo: Coromines and Pascual consider it to reflect the ellipsis of an unattested Late Latin (pertica) mediālis (“pole that goes in the middle of a haystack to hold it together”), with the meaning subsequently transferred to the haystack itself. Compare Portuguese almeara, almeada, and almiare (“outdoor ha

Inherited from Old Spanish adnado, from Late Latin antenātus (“stepson”), from Latin ante nātus (“before birth”); compare Galician enteado, Mirandese antenado, and Portuguese enteado. Doublet of entenado.
From alto (“high”) + -eza, perhaps corresponding to a Late Latin altitia, from Latin altus. Compare Portuguese alteza, Catalan altesa, Italian altezza.
Inherited from Old Spanish ama (“wetnurse”), from Late Latin amma, q.v.
Inherited from Late Latin amāricāre, derived from Latin amārus (“bitter”).
Inherited from Late Latin amīcābilis.
From a- + minorar, from Late Latin minōrāre.

parole.significato: to warn; to reprimand; to admonish
parole.testo: From Late Latin or Vulgar Latin *admonestāre (compare Old French amonester, Portuguese admoestar), from Classical Latin admoneō (“remind, warn”), from ad + moneō (“warn, advise”).
Inherited from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin *amussicāre, from Latin mussāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin anachoreta, from Ancient Greek ἀναχωρητής (anakhōrētḗs).
Borrowed from Late Latin Anacreonticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀνακρέων (Anakréōn), Anacreon a Greek poet.
Borrowed from Late Latin anagramma, from Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “up, back”) + γράμμα (grámma, “letter”).
Borrowed from Late Latin anathema, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνάθεμα (anáthema, “something dedicated, especially dedicated to eternal damnation”), from ἀνᾰτίθημῐ (anătíthēmĭ) + -μᾰ (-mă).
Borrowed from Late Latin anathematīzāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin anatomicus, from Ancient Greek ἀνατομικός (anatomikós), from ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “a cutting up”). See anatomía.
Borrowed from Late Latin angelicus. By surface analysis, ángel (“angel”) + -ico (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: presenter, host (moderator or master of ceremonies for a performance)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin animātor.
Borrowed from Late Latin anxia.
Borrowed from Late Latin antiphrasis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφρασις (antíphrasis).
Borrowed from Late Latin antithesis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + θέσις (thésis, “position, stance”).
Borrowed from Late Latin annuālis, from Latin annuus + -ālis.
From anuo, or borrowed from Late Latin annuārius, from Latin annus. Compare Italian annuario.
Borrowed from Late Latin annuntiātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin anōnymus.
From Late Latin apparātor (literally “preparer”).
Inherited from Late Latin partiārius, from Latin partiō, from pars.

parole.significato: to appear, to turn up, to pop up, to come up
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish aparecer, from Late Latin apparescō, from Latin appāreō + -scō (inchoative suffix).

parole.significato: appellative (of or relating to ascribing names)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin appellatīvus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin apocalypsis, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ποκᾰ́λῠψις (ăpokắlŭpsis, “revelation”).
Inherited from Late Latin apputāre (“to judge”), from ad- (ap) (“to, toward”) + Latin putāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin apologēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογητικός (apologētikós).

Borrowed from Late Latin apologia, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογία (apología, “a speech in defence”), from ἀπόλογος (apólogos, “an account, story”), from ἀπό (apó, “from, off”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech”). In the “expression of remorse” sense, a calque of English apology, and most common in Llanito, consi
Borrowed from Late Latin poplexia or Latin apoplexia, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξίᾱ (apoplēxíā), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō) to cripple by a stroke; ἀπο- (apo-, “from”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostolātus.
Borrowed from Late Latin apothēcārius, based on Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “storehouse”). Doublet of bodeguero and boticario.
Borrowed from Late Latin appretiāre, from Latin pretium. Cognate to English appreciate.

Inherited from Late Latin appectorāre (undergoing metathesis in Old Spanish; compare similar occurrences in pretal, pretil, pretina), from Latin pectus (“chest”). Compare Portuguese apertar, Catalan apitrar.
Borrowed from Late Latin appropriare, from Latin proprius.

parole.significato: apocope (loss or omission of a sound or syllable from the end of a word)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin apocŏpe, from Ancient Greek ἀποκοπή (apokopḗ), ἀποκόπτω (apokóptō, “cut off”).

Borrowed from Late Latin apocryphus (“secret, not approved for public reading”), from Ancient Greek ἀπόκρυφος (apókruphos, “hidden, obscure”), thus "(books) of unknown authorship", from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + κρύπτω (krúptō, “to hide”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostata, from Ancient Greek ἀποστάτης (apostátēs).

Borrowed from Late Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “messenger, one sent forth”), from ἀποστέλλω (apostéllō, “to send off”), from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to set”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostrŏphe, from Ancient Greek ἀποστροφή (apostrophḗ).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostrŏphus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστροφος (apóstrophos).
Inherited from Late Latin arātūra, from Latin arō. Equivalent to arar + -dura. Compare Italian aratura, Romanian arătură.

Inherited from Old Spanish arcidiano, arçidiano, a semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin archidiaconus, based on Ancient Greek ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + διάκονος (diákonos, “servant, minister”). Doublet of archidiácono.
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin archīvum, from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon).
Borrowed from Late Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger, angel”).
Borrowed from Late Latin argūmentātīvus.
Borrowed from Late Latin arōma (“spices”), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma, “seasoning, spicy and/or fragrant smell”).
From Late Latin arōmatīzō.
Borrowed from Late Latin aromăticus. Equivalent to aroma + -ático.
From Late Latin harpa, from Proto-Germanic *harpǭ.
Equivalent to artro- + -itis, from Late Latin arthrītis, from Ancient Greek ἀρθρῖτις (arthrîtis), from ἄρθρον (árthron, “joint”).
From Old Spanish arçobispo, from Late Latin archiepiscopus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιεπίσκοπος (arkhiepískopos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ascēta, from Ancient Greek ἀσκητής (askētḗs).
From Late Latin asphaltum, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt, bitumen”).
Inherited from Late Latin asināricius, from Latin asinus (“donkey”). By surface analysis, asno + -erizo.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin asteriscus, from Ancient Greek ἀστερίσκος (asterískos, “a little star, asterisk”), diminutive of ἀστήρ (astḗr, “star”), used in manuscripts to mark passages.
Inherited from Late Latin astella, from astla, from Latin assula.
Borrowed from Late Latin astrālis, from Latin astrum (“star”).
Borrowed from Late Latin astrologicus, from Ancient Greek ἀστρολογικός (astrologikós). By surface analysis, astrología + -ico.

parole.significato: like this; like that; as such; thus; so; thereby; this way, that way
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish assí, from Late Latin ac sīc. Closely parallel to Portuguese assim, Romanian așa, Aromanian ashi. Compare also Catalan així, French ainsi, Italian così.
Borrowed from Late Latin atticismos.
From Late Latin trānsversāre, modified based on a través de (“across”), from Classical Latin trānsversus. Compare Portuguese atravessar.

parole.significato: a stand for holding books, papers, etc.; music stand; bookstand
parole.testo: From earlier latril, from Late Latin lectorile, from Latin lēctor (“reader”).
Borrowed from Late Latin audibilis. Doublet of oíble.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin augmentāre (“to increase”), from Latin augmentum (“growth, increase”), from augeō (“to increase”). Compare English augment.

parole.significato: to find out, figure out, work out, determine
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish averiguar, from Late Latin vērificāre as a semi-learned term, with the prefix a- from Latin ad-. According to Coromines and Pascual, citing Rufino José Cuervo, it is first attested in a Fuero Juzgo from 1240.

parole.significato: person who takes care of children, tutor
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin avius, masculinized from Latin avia (“grandmother”), whence Spanish aya. Compare Portuguese aio.
Inherited from Old Spanish açuela, from Late Latin asciola, diminutive of ascia (“axe”).
Inherited from Late Latin bassus. Cognate with English base and bass.
Of sound-symbolic origin, possibly via Late Latin *bambalare (“to swing, sway, shake”); compare Portuguese bambolear (“to wobble, waddle”), Norman bamboler and Walloon bamber (“to shake one's head”).

parole.significato: to shuffle (to put in random order)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish barajar (“to quarrel”), from Late Latin baraliare (“dispute, quarrel”), probably from Paleo-Hispanic. Cognate with Portuguese baralhar and Catalan barallar.
Inherited from Late Latin barbus, from Latin barba (“beard”).
Inherited from Old Spanish barca, from Late Latin barca, syncope of Vulgar Latin *bārica, from Latin bāris + Vulgar Latin -ica.

parole.significato: to trumpet (to make an elephant call)
parole.testo: From Late Latin barriō (“to make the sound of an elephant”), from Latin barrus (“elephant”).
Borrowed from Late Latin barytŏnus, from Ancient Greek βαρύτονος (barútonos).
Borrowed from Late Latin benefactor, from Latin benefaciō. Compare the inherited doublet bienhechor.
Borrowed from Late Latin beneplacitum. Cognate with Portuguese beneplácito and Italian beneplacito.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin bēstiālis, from Latin bēstia + -ālis. Equivalent to bestia + -al
Borrowed from Late Latin bibliothēcārius.
Inherited from Old Spanish bienfechor, from or based on Late Latin benefactōrem, from Latin bene (“well”) + factor (“doer”). Compare Portuguese benfeitor and the borrowed doublet benefactor.
Borrowed from Late Latin byzantīnus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin biōticus. By surface analysis, bio- + -t- + -ico.

parole.significato: to blaspheme (to speak against God or religious doctrine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin blasphēmāre. Doublet of lastimar, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Late Latin blasphēmia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía, “slander, blasphemy”).
Borrowed from Late Latin blasphēmus, from Ancient Greek βλάσφημος (blásphēmos).

parole.significato: horn (loud alarm, especially on a motor vehicle)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Late Latin būcina (“trumpet”), probably influenced by boca (“mouth”) or voz (“voice”) in Spanish. Cognate with French buisine (“medieval wind instrument”).
Borrowed from Late Latin bocia.

From earlier brodio via metathesis, from Late Latin brodium, from Frankish *broþ, from Proto-Germanic *bruþą, the same root as English broth. Compare French brouet, Old French breu, Catalan brou, Piedmontese breu, Friulian brût, Sicilian brodu, Italian brodo, Portuguese brodo.

parole.significato: any member of the species Leporinus obtusidens of ray-finned fish (characin)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin bōca, from Ancient Greek βῶκα (bôka), accusative of βῶξ (bôx), a contracted form of βόαξ (bóax), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”).
Inherited from Late Latin bursa. Doublet of bursa. Cognate with English burse (“purse”).

parole.significato: wineskin, bota bag; soft pouch, usually suspended from a cord or lanyard, for carrying wine or other beverages (similar…
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin buttis, with a change of suffix, and probably of Ancient Greek origin. Compare English butt (“large cask”).
Inherited from Late Latin butticula. Doublet of botella, which comes from French bouteille; see also English bottle.

parole.significato: bovine (of, relating to or resembling cattle)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin bovīnus.
Inherited from Late Latin ēbriācus.

parole.significato: crop (pouch-like part of the alimentary tract of some birds)
parole.testo: From Late Latin buccula, from Vulgar Latin *buccula, from Latin bucca. The form was influenced by Old French bouge (“small bag”).

From French bougeron, from Late Latin Bulgarus ("Bulgarian"), used as an insult by the Crusaders, who considered the Bulgarians heretics because of their membership in the Orthodox Church. Cognate with English bugger.
From Late Latin burdus (“bastard, mule”), probably of Celtic origin.

Cognate to Portuguese bordegão, Catalan bordegàs. Of disputed origin. Probably from Late Latin burdus (“bastard”). Inherited from Late Latin burgus, from Frankish *burg (“fortified city”), from Proto-Germanic *burgz (“fortified city”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“high”).
Ultimately from Late Latin burgēnsis, perhaps borrowed from it or via Old French burgeis.
From Late Latin binubus, binūbus (“twice-married man”), derived from Latin bi- (“twice”) + nūbō (“to marry”).
Borrowed from Late Latin bufalus, from Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos, “antelope, wild ox”).

parole.significato: owl, eagle owl (any species of owl from the Strigidae family)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish bufo, from Late Latin būfus, probably of onomatopoeic origin. See also Ancient Greek βοῦφος (boûphos).

parole.significato: to mount an animal, especially a horse
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin caballicāre, from Latin caballus.
Inherited from Late Latin caballāricia, from Latin caballus (“horse”). By surface analysis, caballo + -eriza. Compare Portuguese cavalariça.
Inherited from Late Latin caballāricius, from Latin caballus (“horse”). By surface analysis, caballo + -erizo. Compare Portuguese cavalariço.
From Old Spanish cavallero, inherited from Late Latin caballārius, from Latin caballus. Equivalent to caballo + -ero. Cognate with English cavalier.
From caballero (“horseman, gentleman, cowboy”) + -ía (“-y: forming nouns”), from Late Latin caballārius (“horseman, rider”), from Latin caballus (“horse”) + -ārius (“-ary”).
Inherited from Late Latin caballum (“horse”), from Latin caballum (“pack horse”), of disputed origin. Compare Portuguese cavalo.
Inherited from Old Spanish cabanna, from Late Latin cabanna, capanna, of uncertain origin; possibly a metathesis of Latin canaba. Cognate with Occitan cabana.

parole.significato: body of churchmen that forms the chapter of a cathedral or collegiate church
parole.testo: From Late Latin capitulum, diminutive of Latin caput (“head”). Considering the /i/ < Latin /ĭ/, possibly an early borrowing or otherwise semi-learned (cf. French chapitre). Doublet of capítulo. Compare English chapter.
Inherited from Late Latin caprāricia, from Latin capra (“goat”). By surface analysis, cabra + -eriza.
Inherited from Late Latin caprāricius, from Latin capra (“goat”). By surface analysis, cabra + -erizo.
Inherited from Old Spanish cabruno, from Late Latin caprūnus, from Latin capra or caper.

parole.significato: to fall (to move to a lower position due to gravity)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish caer, from Late Latin cadēre, from Classical Latin cadere. Cognate with French choir, Galician caer, Portuguese cair.
Uncertain. Perhaps from Late Latin *calafodium, based on Latin fodiō (“to dig, bury”).

Inherited from Old Spanish caldera, from Late Latin caldāria, substantivization of the feminine of Latin caldārius, from cal(i)dus (“warm, hot”) + -ārius (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of caldero.

parole.significato: said of someone who likes soups
parole.testo: From Late Latin caldāria, caldārium (“cooking-pot”), derived from Latin caldus (“hot”). Doublet of caldera.
Ultimately from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma), through Late Latin cauma. Possibly through the intermediate of Italian calma, although the word was found in Ibero-Romance as early as in Italian.
Borrowed from Late Latin calvārium.
Inherited from Old Spanish cama, from Late Latin cama, possibly borrowed from Paleo-Hispanic.
Borrowed from Late Latin cambium. Doublet of cambio.
Inherited from Old Spanish camisa.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin camomilla, from Latin chamaemēlon, borrowed from Ancient Greek χᾰμαίμηλον (khămaímēlon).
Inherited from Late Latin campāna.

Inherited from Late Latin campānia (whence also Italian campagna, Portuguese campanha, French champagne), from campāneus, based on Latin campus (“level field”). Doublet of champán or champaña, borrowed from French, and campiña, from Andalusian Arabic.
Inherited from Old Spanish cadnado (with metathesis of /dn/), from Late Latin catēnātum, derived from Latin catēna (“chain”).

Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin canonicus (“canon”), from Ancient Greek κανονικός (kanonikós). Cognate with Portuguese cónego, Galician cóengo. The sense of “corn salad” seems to come by ellipsis from (hierba de los) canónigos.

parole.significato: cloak, cape (a sleeveless garment hanging from the neck)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish capa, from Late Latin cappa. Cognate with English cape and cope (“priestly vestment”). Compare English coping (“top layer of a brick wall”) for an English comparable semantic sense of a "layer".

From Late Latin cappa + an unclear suffix -er- + the suffix -ūcea. Sometimes derived from Medieval Latin caperō (“hood, esp. as worn by monks of the Franciscan order”) (genitive singular caperōnis), but that appears to be a borrowing from Old French chaperon (“hood”), with the same unclear suffix.
Inherited from Late Latin cappella, from the diminutive of cappa.
Borrowed from Late Latin capitāneus, from caput (“head”) + -āneus.
Borrowed from Late Latin capitulum. Compare the inherited doublet of cabildo.

parole.significato: face (the front part of the head)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin cara, from Ancient Greek κάρα (kára, “head, face”).
Inherited from Late Latin calamellus, diminutive of Latin calamus. Doublet of caramelo and the Middle French borrowing churumbela.

parole.significato: to load (to put a load on or in (a means of conveyance or a place of storage))
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin carricāre, from Latin carrus. Compare English charge and French charger. Doublet of carricar.
Borrowed from Late Latin charisma, from Ancient Greek χάρισμα (khárisma, “favorable disposition; grace, favor”), from χάρις (kháris, “favor, grace”), from χαίρω (khaírō, “to be happy”).
Inherited from Late Latin carpa.
Inherited from Late Latin carpentārius (“carpenter”), from Latin carpentārius (“wagon-maker, carriage-maker”).
Inherited from Late Latin (via) carrāria, from Latin carrus. Cognate with English career.
Inherited from Late Latin casālis (“domestic, belonging to the house”) or casāle (“country house, farm”), ultimately from casa. Compare Italian casale, Old French chesal, Catalan casal.
Inherited from Old Spanish casulla (early 13th c.), from Late Latin casubla, an alteration of Latin Latin casula (“little cottage, hooded cloak”), a diminutive of casa (“house”).
Borrowed from Late Latin catacumbae, dissimilation of Latin cata- (“among”) (from Ancient Greek κατά (katá, “under”)) + tumbas.
Inherited from Old Spanish catar, from Late Latin cattāre (“to look at, see”), from Latin captāre (“to strive to see, strive to catch with one's eyes”).
Borrowed from Late Latin catarrhus, from Ancient Greek κατάρροος (katárrhoos, “catarrh, head cold”), from καταρρέω (katarrhéō, “to flow down”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

Learned borrowing from Late Latin catēchūmenus, from Ancient Greek κατηχούμενος (katēkhoúmenos, “being instructed”), present participle passive of κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to sound through, instruct orally”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound, noise”).
Borrowed from Late Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin cathedrālis, from cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρᾱ (kathédrā, “seat”). Equivalent to cátedra + -al.
Borrowed from Late Latin catēgoria, from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (katēgoría).
Borrowed from Late Latin catēchēsis, from Ancient Greek κατήχησις (katḗkhēsis, “oral instruction”), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to instruct orally”).
Borrowed from Late Latin catēchista, from Ancient Greek κατηχιστής (katēkhistḗs, “oral instructor”), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to instruct orally”).

Borrowed from Late Latin catēchizāre (“to teach by word of mouth”), from Ancient Greek κατηχίζω (katēkhízō, “to instruct orally”), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to resound, instruct orally”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound, noise”).

Borrowed from Late Latin ēvāsiōnem (literally “a going out, an escaping”), from Latin ēvāsus, perfect passive participle of ēvādō (“to escape, to go out”), from ē- (“out”) + vādō (“to go; to walk”), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₂dʰ- (“to go”). Cognate with English wade.
Borrowed from Late Latin ēvictiōnem, from Latin ēvincō.
Borrowed from Late Latin excītābilis.

Borrowed from Late Latin exfoliāre (“to strip of leaves”).

Borrowed from Late Latin exorcizāre, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos, “oath”).
Borrowed from Late Latin extēnsīvus, from Latin extēnsus.
From Late Latin extravagantem.

Borrowed from Late Latin fastuōsus, from fāstus (“pride, haughtiness”). Compare Catalan fastuós.

Borrowed from a Late Latin ferālis, from Latin ferus (“wild”), or formed from fiero + -al.

Inherited from Old Spanish fiesta, from Late Latin fĕsta, from Latin fēsta, plural of fēstum. It is unclear why the initial f- stayed in this word instead of becoming the expected h-, perhaps from a learned coloring.

parole.significato: fimbria (structure in the form of a fringe)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin fimbria, from Latin fimbriae. Doublet of franja.
Borrowed from Late Latin physiologicus, from Ancient Greek φυσιολογικός (phusiologikós).

Borrowed from Late Latin fōmentāre, from Latin fōmentum (“lotion”), from fovēre (“heat, cherish”).

Borrowed from Late Latin fortificāre, from Latin fortis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).

parole.significato: fruit (the seed-bearing part of a plant)
parole.testo: From fruto, corresponding to Late Latin frūcta, from Latin frūctus. Compare Portuguese fruta, Catalan fruita, Italian frutta, Sicilian frutta.

Inherited from Old Spanish fuego, from Late Latin focus (“fire”), from Latin focus (“hearth”). The form huego, which began to be used around 1500, was mostly replaced by the form starting with -f-. Inherited from Old Spanish fuerça, from Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”). Compare Portuguese força.
Borrowed from Late Latin fumigātiōnem, from Latin fumigō.

parole.significato: a case, a covering or bag used to wrap something up and protect it
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin funda (“bag”).
Borrowed from Late Latin fūnerālis, from Latin funus.
Borrowed from Late Latin fūnerārius.
Borrowed from Late Latin fūnerārius (“pertaining to a funeral”), from Latin funus. Cognate with English funerary.
Borrowed from Late Latin fustigāre, from Latin fustis. Compare the inherited doublet hostigar.
Inherited from Late Latin garrulāre, denominal from Latin garrulus (“overly talkative”). The verb ultimately replaced Latin garrīre (“to chatter, prattle, waffle”).
Inherited from Late Latin cattus (compare Catalan gat, French chat, Italian gatto, Portuguese gato). See cat for more.
Inherited from Late Latin gaius, from the Roman name Latin Gaius. Also see gaya and urraca.
Borrowed from Late Latin geneālogia, from Ancient Greek γενεαλογία (genealogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”).
Borrowed from Late Latin gibbōsus, from Latin gibbus (“hump”).
Borrowed from Late Latin glandulōsus, from Latin glandula.
Borrowed from Late Latin glōssa, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσᾰ (glôssă).
Inherited from Old Spanish grado, from Late Latin grātum (“act of thanks”), derived from grātus (“pleasant (thing); thankful (person)”), whence also French gré. Doublet of grato, a borrowing.
Inherited from Late Latin grassus. Doublet of craso.

parole.significato: tap, faucet (device used to dispense liquids)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish grifo, a learned borrowing from Late Latin grȳphus (“griffin”), from Latin grȳps, borrowed from Ancient Greek γρῡ́ψ (grū́ps). Noun sense 1 (“faucet”) comes from the ornamentations which fountain faucets commonly bore, which often featured griffin heads. Compare Aragonese j

Inherited from Late Latin gulbia, gubia, from Gaulish *gulbiā, from Proto-Celtic *gulbā, *gulbīnos (“beak, bill”). See the late term for more information. Compare Middle Irish gulba (“beak”), English gouge.
Deverbal from guiñar. Perhaps related to Late Latin cinnus (“scowl, wink”).

parole.significato: Gothic (of or relating to the Goths)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin gothicus (“gothic”).

parole.significato: to habituate; to be inured to, be accustomed to (by habit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin habituāre. Compare English habituate.

parole.significato: falcon (diurnal bird of prey in Falconidae and especially in Falco)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin falcōnem, probably of Germanic origin. Doublet of falcón.
Inherited from Late Latin fastīdiāre, from Latin fastīdiō. Compare the borrowed doublet fastidiar. Compare English fash.
Borrowed from Late Latin hēmistichium, from Ancient Greek ἡμιστίχιον (hēmistíkhion).
Borrowed from Late Latin heptagōnus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἑπτάγωνος (heptágōnos), from ἑπτά (heptá, “seven”) + γωνίᾱ (gōníā, “corner, angle”) + -ος (-os).

Borrowed from Late Latin heteroclitus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερόκλιτος (heteróklitos), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + κλίνω (klínō, “lean, incline”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.
From Late Latin hydromantia, from Ancient Greek ὑδρομαντεία (hudromanteía); corresponding to hidro- + -mancia.
Inherited from Old Spanish ydropisia, from Late Latin hydropisia, from Latin hydropisis, from Ancient Greek ὕδρωψ (húdrōps, “edema”), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”). Compare with English dropsy.
Inherited from Late Latin fīliastrum, from Latin fīlius. Compare Italian figliastro, Romanian fiastru.
Inherited from Late Latin fīlāre. Derivable from hilo + -ar.

parole.significato: knee (joint or the region of the joint in the middle part of the leg between the thigh and the shank)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish ynojo, from Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu.
Borrowed from Late Latin hypnōticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inducing sleep, soporific”).

Borrowed from Late Latin hippocampus (“sea horse”), from Ancient Greek ἱππόκαμπος (hippókampos, “sea horse, hippocamp”, from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) + κάμπος (kámpos, “sea monster”)), describing a mythological creature with a horse's forepart and a fishlike hindquarter.

Borrowed from Late Latin hypocrisis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκρισις (hupókrisis, “answer, stage acting, pretense”), from ῠ̔ποκρῑ́νομαι (hŭpokrī́nomai, “to reply”), from ὑπό (hupó, “under, hypo-”) + the middle voice of κρῑ́νω (krī́nō, “to separate, to judge, to decide”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos, “river horse”).
Borrowed from Late Latin hypothesis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument”).

Inherited from Old Spanish hogaça, from Late Latin focācium (via its plural focācia), derived from Latin focus (“hearth”). Compare Portuguese fogaça. Doublet of focaccia, which was borrowed from Italian.

parole.significato: leaf (usually green and flat organ that is the most prominent feature of most vegetative plants)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish foja, from Late Latin folia, the plural of Classical Latin folium (“leaf”) reinterpreted as a feminine singular noun. Doublet of folio, borrowed from Latin. Cognate with Portuguese folha, Catalan fulla, French feuille, and English foil.
Inherited from Old Spanish folgar, from Late Latin follicāre (“to pant, blow, breathe”), from Latin follis (“bellows”) whence English fool and folly.
Borrowed from Late Latin holocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὁλόκαυστος (holókaustos).
From Late Latin homīlia.

Inherited from an ellipsis of Late Latin pariēs fōrmācea (“a moulded wall”), from fōrmāceus, in reference to its being made by stuffing between two boards. Related to Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “a shape, form”). Reflects pared's change of gender from the original masculine. Compare hormazo and hor
Inherited from Late Latin fōrmācium, substantivised from fōrmāceus (“made in a mould”), related to Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “a shape, form”). Compare hormaza and horma (“dry stone wall”).
Borrowed from Late Latin horripilare.

parole.significato: to host (to perform the role of a host)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin hospitāre (or hospitor, hospitārī), from Latin hospes.
Borrowed from Late Latin hospitāle (“hospice, shelter, guesthouse”), from Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”). Doublet of hostal.
Inherited from Old Spanish fostigar, from Late Latin fūstīgāre, from Latin fūstis. Doublet of fustigar, a borrowing.
Deverbal from holgar, from Late Latin follicāre (“to blow”), from Latin follis. Compare Portuguese folga (“rest; day off”). Doublet of juerga.
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin humiliātiōnem, from humiliō (“to humiliate”).
Altered from Old Spanish homillar, a borrowing from Late Latin humiliāre.

Borrowed from Late Latin Hunnus, from Koine Greek Χοῦνοι (Khoûnoi) or Χουνοί (Khounoí), borrowed through Middle Iranian, apparently ultimately from Turkic *Hun-yü, the name of a tribe (they were known in China as Xiongnu). More at Huns.
Inherited from Late Latin fūrō, from Latin fūror (“to steal”) + -ō. Cognate with English ferret.
Inherited from Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”).  PIE word  *h₃órbʰos
Inherited from Old Spanish figado, from Late Latin fīcatum, ellipsis of Latin iecur fīcātum (literally “figgy liver”), from fīcus (“fig”) + -ātum.
Borrowed from Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “peculiarity; idiom”).
Borrowed from Late Latin illuminātiōnem, from Latin illuminō.

From Late Latin impaenĭtens, equivalent to in- + penitente.
From Late Latin imperturbābilis.
Borrowed from Late Latin impetuosus.
Borrowed from Late Latin implementum, from Latin impleō.

parole.significato: impostor (someone who uses a false identity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin impostor. Cognate with English impostor.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin impostūra.
From impulso, or borrowed from Late Latin impulsāre, from Latin impulsus. Doublet of empujar.
Borrowed from Late Latin inaccessibilis. By surface analysis, in- + accesible.
Borrowed from Late Latin inalienabĭlis, equivalent to in- + alienable.
Borrowed from Late Latin inānītiōnem, from inānīre (“to make empty”), from inānis (“empty, vain”); see inane.
From Late Latin inanimātus.
Borrowed from Late Latin incestuōsus.

From Late Latin incorruptibĭlis.

Borrowed from Late Latin inintellegibilis.

From Late Latin immaterialis.
Borrowed from Late Latin immersiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin innovātiōnem, from Latin innovātus, equivalent to innovar + -ción.

parole.testo: From Late Latin inquilīnātus. By surface analysis, inquilino (“tenant”) + -ato (“-ate”, “-hood”).

Borrowed from Late Latin īnspīrātiōnem, from Latin īnspirō.
Borrowed from Late Latin intellectiōnem, from Latin intellegō or intellectus.

parole.significato: intellect (faculty of knowing, reasoning, and understanding in general)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin intellēctus, from Latin intellegō.
Borrowed from Late Latin interruptor, from Latin interrumpō.

parole.significato: to title (give a title to a work)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin intitulāre.

Borrowed from Late Latin invīsibilis.
From Late Latin invocātor.

parole.significato: to travel; to roam; to be on the road
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin itinerārī, from Latin iter (“road, journey”).

Borrowed from Late Latin iūdaismus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós, “Judaism”), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yehuda, “Judah”).

parole.significato: spree, bender, revel, revelry, carousing, binge, jag
parole.testo: Doublet of huelga, from holgar, from Late Latin follicare (“to blow, breathe”), probably from an Andalusian pronunciation of the word.
Inherited from Old Spanish juramento, juramiento, from Late Latin iūrāmentum, from Latin iūrō. Equivalent to jurar + -mento.
Borrowed from Late Latin iūstificātiōnem, from iūstificō, from Latin iūstus. By surface analysis, justificar + -ción; cognate with Galician xustificación.
Borrowed from Late Latin iūstificāre.
From Late Latin Iutī (plural), from Proto-West Germanic *eut, from Proto-Germanic *eutaz.
From juzga + -dor. Possibly corresponds to Late Latin jūdicātōrem or iūdicātōrem, accusative form of iūdicātor (“judger”), from Latin iūdicō.
Inherited from Late Latin jūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdex (“judge”). Equivalent to juzgar + -miento. Compare Portuguese julgamento, Catalan jutjament, French jugement, Italian giudicamento.
Borrowed from Late Latin labyrinthĭcus, from Latin labyrinthus. By surface analysis, laberinto + -ico.

parole.significato: lip (fleshy protrusion around the opening of the mouth)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin labium. "Labio" replaced "labro" in the 16 C.; compare Old Spanish labro from Latin labrum.
From Late Latin lamentōsus. By surface analysis, lamento + -oso.
Borrowed from Late Latin lanceāre, from Latin lancea. Compare the inherited doublet lanzar.
Inherited from Late Latin lanciārius, from Latin lancea + -ārius. By surface analysis, lanza + -ero.
Inherited from Late Latin lānārius, from Latin lāna; equivalent to lana + -ero.

Inherited from Old Spanish lançar, from Late Latin lanceāre, derived from Latin lancea (“spear”), of Celtiberian origin. Compare Catalan llançar, Asturian llanzar, French lancer, Italian lanciare, Occitan and Portuguese lançar, English launch. Doublet of lancear, a later borrowing.
Inherited from Late Latin blastēmāre (variant of blasphēmāre). Doublet of blasfemar, which was borrowed from Latin.
From lavar + -dero, possibly corresponding to Late Latin lavātōrium, from Latin lavō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin lavātōrium.
From Late Latin canis leporārius, from Latin lepus (“hare”). By surface analysis, liebre + -ero. Doublet of lebrel (“sighthound, whippet”).
From Late Latin lecanomantia, from Ancient Greek λεκανομαντείᾱ (lekanomanteíā, “lekanomanteía”), from λεκάνη (lekánē, “dish, pan”) + -mancia.

Inherited from Old Spanish leche, from an earlier *leite < *laite, from Late Latin lactem m or f, from Latin lac n, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵlákts. Compare Galician and Portuguese leite m and French lait m.
Borrowed from Late Latin lēctūra, from Latin lēctūrus.
Borrowed from Late Latin lēgislātiōnem (“the giving of the law”); By surface analysis, legislar + -ción.

parole.significato: legua, Spanish league (a traditional unit of distance equivalent to about 4.2 km)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin leuga and leuca (“Gaulish league, distance of one hour's walking”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *lougā. Cognate with Galician legua, Portuguese légua, and Catalan llegua.
Borrowed from Late Latin leopardus, from Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos), from λέων (léōn, “lion”) + πάρδος (párdos, “male panther”), a later form of πάρδαλις (párdalis, “leopard”).
Uncertain; presumably from Late Latin lurdus (“slow; stupid”), often suggested to be derived from Latin lūridus (“sallow, pale”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin litanīa, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía, “prayer”), from λιτή (litḗ, “supplication”).

parole.significato: leviathan (a sea monster of tremendous strength)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin leviathan, a biblical transliteration of Hebrew לִוְיָתָן (liv'yatán, “whale”).
Borrowed from Late Latin Levīta.
Borrowed from Late Latin levisticum, probably an alteration of Latin ligusticum, from Ligusticus (“Ligurian”), ultimately from Ancient Greek Λίγυς (Lígus).
Borrowed from Late Latin liquefactiōnem, from Latin liquefaciōnem (“to melt, to liquify”).
Inherited from Late Latin lendinem, from Latin lendem.
From ligar + -ción, or borrowed from Late Latin ligātiōnem. Doublet of ligazón.
Borrowed from Late Latin ligātūra, from Latin ligātus, perfect passive participle of ligō (“to tie”).
Borrowed from Late Latin litterālis.
Borrowed from Late Latin lītūrgia, from Ancient Greek λειτουργία (leitourgía).
Inherited from Late Latin lupicĭnus, from Latin lupus; equivalent to lobo (“wolf”) + -ezno.
Borrowed from Late Latin locālis, from Latin locus. Compare the inherited doublet lugar.
Inherited from Late Latin langobardus, of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *langabardaz.
From Late Latin lucernarium.
Inherited from Late Latin lucta, from Latin luctor (whence English reluctant and ineluctable). Compare Catalan lluita, Galician loita, French lutte, Italian lotta and Romanian luptă.
From older logar, from Old Spanish logar, from Late Latin locālem, from Latin locus. Doublet of local.

Inherited from Old Spanish lumbrera, lumnera, from Late Latin lūmināria (compare Galician lumieira, Catalan llumenera (“oil lamp, luminary”), French lumière (“light”), Romanian lumânare (“candle”)), plural of lūmināre (“light, lamp, luminary”), based on Latin lūmen (“light”). Borrowed from Late Latin lūmināria, neuter plural of lūmināre, from Latin lūmen. Compare the inherited doublet lumbrera.
From Late Latin lunatiō.
From lámpada, from Late Latin lampăda, from Latin lampas.
Borrowed from Late Latin logicus.
From Late Latin Madianīta, from Hebrew מדיינים. Equivalent to Madián + -ita.
Inherited from Late Latin mātrastra (“stepmother”), from Latin māter (“mother”). Compare Portuguese madrasta, Catalan madrastra.

Inherited from Late Latin mātrīcāria (“related to the womb”), from Latin mātrīx (“womb”). The semantic development could mirror the one in cunīculus (“underground tunnel; rabbit”) if indeed related to cunnus (“vagina”).
Borrowed from Late Latin magīa, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía).
Inherited from Old Spanish maldat, from Late Latin malitātem, from Latin malus. Equivalent to mal + -dad. Compare Portuguese maldade.
Inherited from Old Spanish malfechor, from Late Latin malefactōrem, from Latin malefaciō. Compare Portuguese malfeitor.
Borrowed from Late Latin mammothreptus.
Borrowed from Late Latin manifestātiōnem.
Inherited from Late Latin manuc(u)lus, modified ultimately from Latin manipulus. Compare Portuguese molho.

Inherited from Late Latin manūtenēre (“to support”), from Latin manū (“with the hand”) + teneō (“to hold”). Equivalent to mano + tener. Compare Galician and Portuguese manter, French maintenir, Italian mantenere.
Inherited from Late Latin mantum, back-formation from mantellum, ultimately from Gaulish [Term?].
Borrowed from Late Latin manna, from Ancient Greek μάννα (mánna), from Hebrew מָן (mān).
Borrowed from Late Latin maniacus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”). See manía.

From Late Latin mīrābilia (“wonder”), substantivization of the neuter plural of Latin mīrābilis (“wonderful”). Old Spanish also had maravija, with the expected outcome of the Latin ending.
